title: Prepositions of time and place
tagline: At six, on Monday, in May: the small words for time and place.
why: Prepositions are tiny but everywhere: at, on and in change meaning completely, and verbs like listen and wait need their own partner word. In Listening Part 2 you'll hear times and dates fast, and in Reading Part 5 one wrong preposition means a wrong answer.

hook.text: It's Liam's first day. "Your classroom is next to the library," says Nadia. "Lessons start at eight, and football club is on Fridays." Liam looks confused: "So many small words!"
hook.ask: Next to, at and on are all small words that tell you where or when. Can you match each one to time or place?

diagrams.title: Verbs with their own preposition
diagrams.caption: Some verbs and their preposition are best learnt together, like one long word: listen-to, wait-for, look-at.

examples.text: My birthday is on the third of May.
The shop is open from nine to five.
examples.note: from…to shows the start and end

examples.text: We stayed at my grandma's house for two weeks during the holidays.
examples.note: for + a length of time, during + an event

examples.text: The bank is opposite the school, next to the bakery.
examples.note: opposite = across from; next to = right beside

examples.text: Liam is sitting between Sofia and Nadia.
examples.note: between = with one thing on each side

examples.text: I always listen to music on the bus.

watch_out.wrong: I wake up in six o'clock.
watch_out.why: Exact clock times always use at.
Days of the week use on, not in.
Listen always needs to before the thing you hear.
Wait always needs for before the thing you're waiting for.

watch_out.wrong: The bank is opposite to the school.
watch_out.why: Opposite doesn't need to after it.

l1.why: Exact clock times use at, never in.
Spanish escuchar has no preposition, but English listen always needs to.
Months use in, not at — even though Spanish en can feel like at.
Spanish esperar has no preposition, but English wait always needs for.

remember.trick: AT a point, ON a day or surface, IN a space or period.
remember.tip: Think of at as a tiny dot (6 o'clock, the bus stop), on as a flat line or day (Monday, the wall), and in as a box (May, the kitchen).

dialogue.title: Finding your way around
dialogue.context: It's Liam's first week. Nadia shows him around the school and explains the timetable.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Your classroom is next to the library, opposite the school office.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It's behind the gym, between the music room and the art room.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Thanks. What time do lessons start?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: We start at eight o'clock, and we have lunch at half past twelve.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: And the football club — is it on Fridays?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes, on Fridays, from four to five. You should listen to the announcements in the morning.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Great, I'll wait for you at the gate tomorrow!

can_do: I can use at, on and in for the right kind of time and place.
I can use next to, opposite, between, behind and in front of to describe where things are.
I can use the right preposition after verbs like listen to, wait for and look at.
summary: Use at for an exact time or a point in place: at 6 o'clock, at school.
Use on for days, dates and surfaces: on Monday, on the wall.
Use in for months, years, seasons and spaces: in May, in the kitchen.
Some verbs always need a preposition: listen to, wait for, look at — learn them together as one chunk.
